title: What is serialized data, how does serialization/deserialization work, and why must a class implement `Serializable`?
shortTitle: What is serialized data, how serialization works, and why a class must implement Serializable

s1_definition.profdef: Serialization is the process of converting a live Java object, which exists as a graph of references in heap memory, into a flat sequence of bytes that captures the object's state so it can be stored on disk, cached, or transmitted over a network. Deserialization is the reverse process that reads those bytes and reconstructs an equivalent object graph in memory. Serialized data is that resulting byte stream, which encodes the class identity, a version identifier, and the values of all non-static, non-transient fields, recursively including referenced objects. A class must implement the Serializable marker interface to opt in, because the serialization machinery refuses to serialize an object whose class is not Serializable, throwing NotSerializableException; the interface carries no methods and acts purely as a permission flag signaling that the author intends instances to be safely convertible to bytes.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a live object is like a customer's file spread open on a desk with sticky notes pointing to other related files. Serialization is like carefully flattening that whole spread, along with the connected files it points to, into a single sealed envelope of paper that can be mailed to another branch or filed in the archive. Deserialization is the receiving branch opening the envelope and laying the files back out on a desk exactly as they were, with the sticky-note links restored. The sealed envelope of paper is the serialized data. The Serializable interface is like a signed consent form the file's owner must attach saying this file is approved to be flattened and mailed; without that consent form the mail room refuses to flatten it, because sending a file that was never cleared for transport could expose or corrupt sensitive records.
s1_definition.oneliner: Serialization flattens a live object graph into a byte stream and deserialization rebuilds it, and a class must implement the Serializable marker interface to grant permission, or the machinery throws NotSerializableException.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Serialization is the process of converting a live Java object, which exists as a graph of references in heap memory, into a flat sequence of bytes that captures the object's state so it can be stored on disk, cached, or transmitted over a network. Deserialization is the reverse process that reads those bytes and reconstructs an equivalent object graph in memory. Serialized data is that resulting byte stream, which encodes the class identity, a version identifier, and the values of all non-static, non-transient fields, recursively including referenced objects. A class must implement the Serializable marker interface to opt in, because the serialization machinery refuses to serialize an object whose class is not Serializable, throwing NotSerializableException; the interface carries no methods and acts purely as a permission flag signaling that the author intends instances to be safely convertible to bytes.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a live object is like a customer's file spread open on a desk with sticky notes pointing to other related files. Serialization is like carefully flattening that whole spread, along with the connected files it points to, into a single sealed envelope of paper that can be mailed to another branch or filed in the archive. Deserialization is the receiving branch opening the envelope and laying the files back out on a desk exactly as they were, with the sticky-note links restored. The sealed envelope of paper is the serialized data. The Serializable interface is like a signed consent form the file's owner must attach saying this file is approved to be flattened and mailed; without that consent form the mail room refuses to flatten it, because sending a file that was never cleared for transport could expose or corrupt sensitive records.

**One line to remember:** Serialization flattens a live object graph into a byte stream and deserialization rebuilds it, and a class must implement the Serializable marker interface to grant permission, or the machinery throws NotSerializableException.

sections.s2_technical:
A Java object in memory is a structure of fields, some holding primitives and some holding references to other objects, forming a graph. Serialization walks that graph starting from the root object and writes a byte representation: it records the class name and its serialVersionUID, then each non-static, non-transient field, and for reference fields it recursively serializes the referenced objects, so the entire reachable graph is captured. This is done through an ObjectOutputStream, for example `oos.writeObject(account)`, which produces the serialized bytes.

Deserialization through an ObjectInputStream reads the bytes back, as in `Account a = (Account) ois.readObject()`. It reads the class identity, verifies the serialVersionUID matches the loaded class, allocates the object without calling a constructor, and fills in the fields from the stream, recursively reconstructing referenced objects and restoring the shared-reference structure so that if two fields pointed to the same object before, they point to the same reconstructed object after.

A class must implement Serializable because the machinery checks for it as a permission flag. Serializable is a marker interface with no methods; its only purpose is to declare that the author permits instances to be serialized. If you try to serialize an object whose class does not implement Serializable, the stream throws NotSerializableException naming the offending class. This opt-in design exists because blindly serializing arbitrary objects would be unsafe: objects may hold resources, secrets, or state that is meaningless or dangerous to persist, so the language requires the author to consciously declare serializability.

Several important mechanics follow. The serialVersionUID is a version number for the class; if a serialized stream's id does not match the current class's id, deserialization throws InvalidClassException, which protects against reading bytes written by an incompatible class version. Declaring it explicitly, as `private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;`, gives you control over compatibility; relying on the auto-generated value is brittle because it changes with almost any class modification. Transient fields are skipped and static fields are not serialized because they belong to the class. The entire referenced graph must be serializable, so every referenced object's class must also implement Serializable or be transient, or serialization fails.

Several senior points matter. First, deserialization does not run constructors, so invariants enforced only in a constructor can be bypassed, which is a well-known security concern; untrusted serialized data can be a serious vulnerability, so you must never deserialize data from an untrusted source without strict controls, and modern guidance strongly favors safer formats. Second, because native serialization is fragile across versions and risky with untrusted input, most banking systems use explicit, schema-controlled formats such as JSON or protocol buffers for persistence and messaging, reserving native serialization for controlled internal uses like certain caches or RMI. Third, you can customize the process with writeObject and readObject for validation, or use readResolve to enforce singletons. Fourth, sensitive fields must be transient and still protected on other paths, since serialization is one more place data can escape. The practical message is that serialization is a powerful way to persist and transmit object state, Serializable is the required opt-in permission, serialVersionUID governs version compatibility, and native serialization must be used carefully and never on untrusted input.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank wants to cache a full account object, including its referenced owner object, by writing it to a byte store and reading it back later. This is exactly serialization and deserialization of an object graph.

Problem 2 — A developer tried to serialize an account whose referenced owner class did not implement Serializable, and it failed with NotSerializableException. This is exactly why every class in the reachable graph must implement Serializable.

Problem 3 — After changing the account class, old cached bytes failed to load with an InvalidClassException until a stable serialVersionUID was declared. This is exactly the role of serialVersionUID in version compatibility.

The code defines a Serializable `Account` referencing a Serializable `Owner`, with a declared serialVersionUID and a transient sensitive field, and a `SerializationDemo` main class that serializes and deserializes Rajesh's account graph and shows the behavior.

```
│       ├── Owner.java               (Serializable — referenced object)
│       ├── Account.java             (Serializable — root object, references Owner)
```

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/Owner.java \
             src/main/java/com/bank/core/Account.java \

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.core.SerializationDemo
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account with a balance and a referenced owner object, plus a transient session token.

Step 1 — The account object is created in memory, holding a reference to the owner object, forming a small graph. The account also holds a transient session token.

Step 2 — Serialization begins at the account. The machinery checks that Account implements Serializable, which it does, then writes the class identity and serialVersionUID, then the account id and balance. When it reaches the owner reference, it checks that Owner is Serializable, which it is, and recursively serializes the owner's fields into the same stream, so the whole graph is captured in one byte sequence. The transient session token is skipped.

Step 3 — The resulting bytes are a flat representation of both the account and the owner, with their link encoded. This is the serialized data that could be stored or transmitted.

Step 4 — Deserialization reads the bytes. It verifies the serialVersionUID matches the current Account class, allocates an account without calling its constructor, fills in the account id and balance, and when it encounters the owner it reconstructs the owner object and links it back, restoring the graph structure.

Step 5 — The restored account has its id, balance, and owner intact, proving the recursive reconstruction. The session token is null because it was transient and never written, so it must be re-established separately.

Step 6 — The output shows the full graph surviving the round trip, the owner correctly restored through recursion, and the transient token gone, demonstrating what serialized data is, how the round trip works, and that implementing Serializable on both classes made it possible.

```
Oct 30, 2026 6:22:09 PM com.bank.core.SerializationDemo main
INFO: BEFORE: account=SAV2001 balance=1000000.00 owner=Rajesh Kumar sessionToken=live-session-xyz
INFO: Serialized object graph into 212 bytes.
INFO: AFTER: account=SAV2001 balance=1000000.00 owner=Rajesh Kumar (owner restored recursively)
WARNING: AFTER: sessionToken=null (null — transient, not serialized)
INFO: Serializable opt-in + matching serialVersionUID made this round trip work.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  In-memory object graph
   Account(SAV2001, balance=1,000,000) ──owner──→ Owner("Rajesh Kumar","ABCDE1234F")
            transient sessionToken="live-session-xyz"
    │
    ▼ writeObject (ObjectOutputStream) — walks the graph
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ BYTE STREAM (serialized data)                              │
  │  [Account class + serialVersionUID]                        │
  │   accountId ✓  balance ✓  owner→[Owner class, name, pan] ✓ │
  │   sessionToken ✗ (transient)                               │
  └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ readObject (ObjectInputStream)
                              │  verify serialVersionUID, allocate (no ctor), fill fields
                              ▼
  Reconstructed graph
   Account(SAV2001, 1,000,000) ──owner──→ Owner("Rajesh Kumar", ...)
            sessionToken = null (transient)

  If Owner NOT Serializable → NotSerializableException
  If serialVersionUID mismatch → InvalidClassException
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Serialization & Serializable ═══

  ┌─ Key Rules ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Serialization: object graph → byte stream (reachable, recursive)  │
  │  Deserialization: bytes → object graph (NO constructor called)     │
  │  Serializable = marker interface = permission to serialize         │
  │  non-Serializable in graph → NotSerializableException              │
  │  serialVersionUID: version check → mismatch = InvalidClassException│
  │  static not serialized; transient skipped                          │
  │  NEVER deserialize untrusted data (security risk)                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each class owns its own serializable state                     │
  │  L: Serializable contract honored by Account and Owner             │
  │  D: cache depends on Serializable abstraction, not concrete store  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ Account : Serializable        │ owner  │   Owner : Serializable    │
  │ ───────────────────────────── │───────▶│ ───────────────────────── │
  │ - serialVersionUID = 1L       │  1  1  │ - serialVersionUID = 1L   │
  │ - accountId: String           │        │ - name: String            │
  │ - balance: BigDecimal         │        │ - panId: String           │
  │ - transient sessionToken      │        └───────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: object across serialize round trip ─────────────

  [live graph in heap]
       │ writeObject (check Serializable, walk graph)
       ▼
  [byte stream: class + UID + non-transient fields, recursive]
       │ readObject (verify UID, allocate w/o ctor, fill)
       ▼
  [reconstructed graph: refs restored, transient = default]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. writeObject(account) → check Serializable
  2. write Account fields → reach owner → recurse into Owner
  3. skip transient sessionToken
  4. readObject → verify serialVersionUID
  5. allocate Account (no ctor) → fill → reconstruct Owner
  6. sessionToken = null (transient)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Serialization is the process of converting a live Java object, which in memory is a graph of fields and references, into a flat sequence of bytes that captures its state so it can be stored, cached, or sent over a network. Deserialization is the reverse: it reads those bytes and rebuilds an equivalent object graph in memory. The serialized data itself is that byte stream, which encodes the class identity, a version identifier, and the values of all non-static, non-transient fields, recursively including every object the root refers to, so the whole reachable graph is captured.

The mechanics are straightforward. I write an object through an ObjectOutputStream, which walks the graph from the root, records each class and its serialVersionUID, writes the ordinary fields, and recursively serializes referenced objects, preserving shared references. I read it back through an ObjectInputStream, which verifies the serialVersionUID against the current class, allocates the object without calling any constructor, fills in the fields, and reconstructs the referenced objects and their links. In our banking system a good example is caching an account object that references an owner object; serializing the account automatically captures the owner too, and deserializing restores both with their link intact, while a transient session token is skipped and returns null.

A class must implement Serializable because the machinery treats it as a permission flag. Serializable is a marker interface with no methods, and its only job is to let the author declare that instances may be serialized. If I try to serialize an object whose class, or any class in its referenced graph, does not implement Serializable, the stream throws a NotSerializableException naming the offending class. This opt-in exists for safety, because blindly flattening arbitrary objects that may hold resources or secrets would be dangerous, so the language insists the author consciously grant permission. I learned this concretely when an account failed to serialize until its referenced owner class also implemented the interface.

The senior points I stress are these. The serialVersionUID is a version number for the class, and if the stream's id does not match the current class, deserialization throws InvalidClassException, which is why I always declare a stable serialVersionUID explicitly rather than relying on the brittle auto-generated value that changes with almost any edit. Deserialization does not run constructors, so invariants enforced only in a constructor can be bypassed, which makes deserializing untrusted data a serious security risk, and for that reason modern banking systems prefer explicit, schema-controlled formats like JSON or protocol buffers for persistence and messaging and reserve native serialization for controlled internal uses. I also keep sensitive fields transient and protected on every other path, and I never deserialize bytes from an untrusted source. So my complete answer is that serialization flattens an object graph into bytes and deserialization rebuilds it, Serializable is the mandatory opt-in permission enforced by NotSerializableException, serialVersionUID governs version compatibility, and native serialization is powerful but must be used carefully and never on untrusted input.
